Article.ArticleTitle: Novel genes and regulators that influence production of cell surface exopolysaccharides in Sinorhizobium meliloti.

Abstract.AbstractText: Sinorhizobium meliloti is a soil-dwelling α-proteobacterium that engages in a nitrogen-fixing root nodule symbiosis with leguminous plants. Cell surface polysaccharides are important for both adapting to stresses in the soil and development of an effective symbiotic interaction. Among the polysaccharides characterized to date, the acidic exopolysaccharides EPS-I (succinoglycan) and EPS-II (galactoglucan) are particularly important for protection from abiotic stresses, biofilm formation, root colonization, and infection of plant roots. Previous genetic screens discovered mutants impaired in EPS production, allowing delineation of EPS biosynthetic pathways. Here we report on a genetic screen to isolate mutants with mucoid colonial morphologies that imply overproduction of EPS. Screening with Tn5-110, which allows recovery of both null and upregulation mutants, yielded 47 mucoid mutants, most of which overproduce EPS-I; among the 30 unique genes and intergenic regions identified, 14 have not been previously associated with EPS production. We identified a new protein-coding gene, emmD, which may be involved in regulation of EPS-I production as part of the EmmABC three-component regulatory circuit. We also identified a mutant defective in EPS-I production, motility, and symbiosis, where Tn5-110 was unlinked to the mutant phenotypes; these phenotypes result from a missense mutation in rpoA corresponding to the domain of the RNA polymerase α-subunit known to interact with transcription regulators.IMPORTANCE The α-proteobacterium Sinorhizobium meliloti converts dinitrogen to ammonium while inhabiting specialized plant organs termed root nodules. Transformation of S. meliloti from a free-living soil bacterium to a nitrogen-fixing plant symbiont is a complex developmental process requiring close interaction between the two partners. As the interface between the bacterium and its environment, the S. meliloti cell surface plays a critical role in adaptation to varied soil environments and interaction with plant hosts. We isolated and characterized S. meliloti mutants with increased production of exopolysaccharides, key cell surface components. Our diverse set of mutants suggests roles for exopolysaccharide production in growth, metabolism, cell division, envelope homeostasis, biofilm formation, stress response, motility, and symbiosis.
